newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bids for Van Gogh painting fall short in Paris sale.
newsitem.headline: Bids for Van Gogh painting fall short in Paris sale.

text.p: A Paris auction house failed to sell one of Vincent Van Gogh's last paintings on Tuesday when bidding reached only 32 million francs ($6.1 million), short of the minimum price set for its sale.
Buyers competed for the masterpiece in hushed bidding at the plush Georges V Hotel in Paris, but auctioneer Jacques Tajan concluded that the reserve price had not been reached.
Art experts predicted before the auction it might fetch as much as 50 to 60 million francs ($9.5 to $11.4 million).
The price of Jardin a Auvers (Garden at Auvers), painted in July 1890 just before the Dutch artist's suicide, might have been much higher on the international market.
But its market value was considerably reduced after the French Culture Ministry declared the painting a national treasure, effectively banning its sale outside France.
"I'm distressed...The state did not even take part in the bidding," Tajan said.
He said he hoped Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy might take up negotiations about a possible purchase that would allow it to hang in Paris' Musee d'Orsay on the Left Bank.
"This painting is a Franco-French work which cannot leave the country. It's not a great incentive (to buy) in a country like France, going through a crisis, with many people out of work," he said.

The daily Liberation dubbed the work the "cursed painting" because of controversies over the export ban and also due to media questions about the authenticity of the most accomplished oil painting from the last feverish days of Van Gogh's life.
Art historians are all but unanimous in declaring the work authentic despite a media controversy in France.
The painting, showing a garden full of swirling greens and blues with red flowers, was bought in 1992 by banker Jean-Marc Vernes for 55 million francs ($10.4 million) from collector Jacques Walter.
Walter successfully sued the state for imposing the export ban, arguing it slashed the painting's value at auctions since his family acquired it in 1955.

The Supreme Court in February 1996 awarded Walter 145 million francs ($27.5 million) compensation -- 2.5 francs (50 cts) for each of France's 58 million inhabitants -- in a ruling that has dampened Paris's efforts to prevent the flight of other French masterpieces.
Many art lovers and commentators had urged the state to buy the painting, but the identity of the bidders was not immediately clear.
Debate about the work's authenticity started with a critic of the conservative daily Le Figaro, Jean-Marie Tasset.

Tasset has argued the painting is too polished, does not feature in correspondence between Van Gogh and his brother Theo and might just come from a collection of a friend of Van Gogh, Claude Emile Schuffenecker, who copied masterpieces.
